added_lines: there are some weeks when the gospel seems to meet us exactly where we are. this is one of those weeks. over recent days, many of us have been shocked and de eply disturbed by the loss of live of four members of a family in waterford. i n times like these, people can find themselves searching for answers and struggling to understand why suffering occurs. in the face of such evil and suffering, many people ask difficult questions. where was god?how can something so terrible happen? how are we me ant to make sense of such cruelty? these are not new questions. they are questions that faithful people have asked for centuries. even jesus , hanging on the cross, cried out in anguish. faith does not remove pain, nor does it provide simple answers to life's darkest moments. the gospel today reminds us that we live in this world, but we belong ultimately to god. yet our world often feels overwhelmed by fea r, violence, anger, and division. many people are carrying anxieties about their families, their future, and the safety of their communities. we are more connect ed than ever through television, smartphones, and social media, yet many people feel more worried, isolated, and burdened than ever before. part of the challenge is what many call "information overload." within minutes of a tragedy occurring, we are inundated with images, c ommentary, speculation, and endless updates. while it is important to stay infor med, there comes a point when constant exposure to distressing news begins to weigh heavily on our minds and spirits. we find ourselves absorbing fear that we do little about. as christians, we are not called to ignore the suffe ring of the world. we are called to pray, to care, and to act where we can. but neithe r are we called to carry the weight of every tragedy alone. sometimes caring for our spiritual wellbeing means stepping away from the endless news cycle, tur ning off our phones for a while, spending time with family, taking a walk, pr aying quietly, or simply sitting in god's presence. continued back page… st. colman’s parish 29th sunday in ordinary time 17th/18th october 2026 milltown

the evil we witness can tempt us to despair, but de spair is never the christian response. our response is hope. not a naïve hope that ignores reality, but a hope rooted in the belief that goodness is stronger than hatred, light is stronger than darkness, and love is stronger than death. perhaps this week's tragedy reminds us of what truly matters. life is precious and fragile. the arguments, jealousies, resentments , and worries that consume so much of our energy suddenly seem less important. what remains important are the relationships we nurture, the kindness we show , and the love we share with those closest to us. as we gather for mass this weekend, let us pray for all affected by the tragedy in waterford, for those who live in fear, for emerge ncy responders, and for all who struggle to find hope in difficult times. may go d help us to be people of peace in an anxious world, people of compassion in a hurting world, and people of hope in a world that desperately needs it. lord of all compassion, we pray for all of those caught up in the midst of tragedy. for those who have lost life and those working to save life. for those who are worried for people they love. for those who will see their loved ones no longer. for those in need of the peace that passes all understanding. for all who turn to you in the midst of turmoil. for those who cry out to you in fear and in love. for those in confusion and those in despair. for those whose tears are yet to dry. for those in need of your unending love. amen. last weekend’s offertory collection: €990.00 thank you for your generosity and continued support! killorglin pastoral area priest on duty this weekend kevin sullivan (087) 6277 638
